en: *An Exposition of the Essential Meaning of the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom*,
composed by the Bodhisattva Śrāmaṇera Zhixu.
This work directly points out that the present, single thought-moment of our own "mediocre" mind is itself the three kinds of *prajñā*.

Now, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are three things without distinction. However, because the phenomena of sentient beings are too vast and the teachings of the Buddha are too sublime, it is easier for those at the initial stage of practice to contemplate the mind alone.

Therefore, although this great compendium of over six hundred fascicles extensively elucidates Prajñā by means of both the Buddha-dharma and the dharma of sentient beings, we shall now directly reveal Prajñā solely through the dharma of the mind.
Furthermore, although the *Mahāvaipulya* scriptures extensively elucidate the dharmas of the Buddha and the dharmas of sentient beings, they never do so apart from the dharmas of the mind.
Likewise, although the present text directly elucidates the dharmas of the mind, it never fails to encompass the dharmas of the Buddha and the dharmas of sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the "Threefold Non-differentiation. This is because the present, single thought-moment of our own—the subtle and responsive mind—is empty and luminous.
It is thoroughly penetrating; it is clear and constantly aware, abiding in none of the various locations—neither within, without, nor in between—and it leaves no trace of past, present, or future.
This is precisely the *prajñā* of contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*).

By means of our present single thought—the momentary mind—it vividly manifests the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world, even unto the ten realms and the provisional or real lands, holding them all with equal seal.
Neither preceding nor following, they are simultaneously and instantaneously complete; this is precisely the *prajñā* of letters (*vyañjana-prajñā*).
For all realms—mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness—their nature is nothing other than letters.
It is not only paper, ink, and speech that constitute letters. This includes everything possessed by the present, infinitesimal thought of each person.
The nature of cognition and the nature of its objects are without division or distinction; there is neither subject nor object, neither right nor wrong.
They are unified within the single substance of the Dharma-realm, which is precisely the prajñā of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā). This is the prajñā of the true mark.
Neither the other shore nor this shore—by penetrating the true reality (*dharmatā*) of this present single thought-moment, birth-and-death is itself nirvana;
this is called a *pāramitā*. Contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*) is also neither the other shore nor this shore;
by illuminating that this present single thought-moment is itself true reality, delusion is immediately transformed into wisdom; this is called a *pāramitā*. As for the wisdom of letters...
If it is neither the other shore nor this shore, it reveals that this present single thought-moment is itself the true aspect (dharmatā).

Therefore, karma and affliction are themselves liberation; this is called the *pāramitā*. Consequently, this mind is the three kinds of *prajñā*, and the three kinds of *prajñā* are simply this one mind.
This principle is eternally thus and cannot be altered; therefore, it is called a *sūtra*. Relying upon this—
It is the practice accomplished by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time; therefore, it is called a *sūtra*.
When this Dharma-gate is expounded, neither celestial Māras nor non-Buddhist paths can disturb or destroy it; therefore, it is called a *sūtra*.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby transcending all suffering and calamity.
To know the path down the mountain, one must ask those who have already traversed it; therefore, this example is cited as a model for those who have perfected the practice of contemplating the mind.

It is likewise so. "Contemplation" refers to the wisdom capable of observing; it is precisely the threefold contemplation within a single mind, collectively termed the *prajñā* of contemplative illumination (*guan-chaog*).
"Sovereignty" means that by realizing the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*), one attains great liberation amidst all objective realms.
A *bodhisattva* (菩薩) is one who awakens sentient beings; it is a title for one who benefits both self and others. When wisdom accords with the true reality (*dharmatā*), self-benefit is fulfilled;
when wisdom is expressed through words and letters, benefit for others becomes universal. Thus, one is named a *bodhisattva*. This clarifies the person capable of such practice.
As for "the profound *prajñāpāramitā*," the three types of wisdom are attained within a single moment of mind. Expedient...
Because it cannot be shared with those taught in the three vehicles, it is called "profound. This generally clarifies the Dharma that is practiced. Regarding "time":

this refers retrospectively to the periods prior to vast eons. From the moment one attains corresponding realization once, one proceeds directly until the end of the future limit, never departing from profound *prajñā* from beginning to end.
"Illuminatively seeing" specifically clarifies the subject that contemplates.

This wisdom is the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*āloka-prajñā*). The "five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*) specifically clarify the objects of observation, which is the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*).

"All are empty" specifically clarifies the truth that is revealed, which is the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*). The five aggregates are none other than emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;

they are entirely free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and their nature transcends the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*). They are merely designated by the forced name "emptiness. To cross over...
All those who suffer from afflictions and calamities emerge of their own accord from the causes and effects of the two deaths;

they also cause all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm to likewise emerge from the causes and effects of the two deaths. This is precisely the efficacy of practicing the Dharma, and it is also the *pāramitās*.
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Śāriputra, this mark of the emptiness of all dharmas is neither born nor extinguished;
it is neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, within emptiness there is no form; there is no feeling, perception, mental formation, or consciousness; there is no eye.
No ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; no eye-element, and so forth, up to no consciousness-element.
No ignorance, nor the extinction of ignorance; and so forth, up to no old age and death, nor the extinction of old age and death.
No suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path. No wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to be attained.
This extensively explains the truth of the realm wherein the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all empty, and within which contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) exercises mastery.
Since this realm of truth cannot be fully realized without contemplative observation, as for the mind: if it does not arise, that is one thing;

yet, were there even a momentary arising of thought, the sense-faculties, the personal body, and the objective world would necessarily manifest instantaneously. This is termed the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), and it must necessarily experience and receive all [sensory objects].

The objective spheres of suffering and pleasure are called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*); that which necessarily grasps signs and establishes names and conventions is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*);
that which necessarily arises and ceases, flowing and shifting without rest, is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);

and that which necessarily and clearly discriminates all phenomena is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Thus, one should know that according to whatever momentary thought arises, it naturally and inherently possesses [all five aggregates].
The five aggregates are turbid and confused; now, by illuminating them with the profound *prajñā*, one realizes that form is nothing but mind and that there is no separate, real form.
All sense-faculties, bodies, and the vessel-world are like flowers in the sky or objects in a dream. Therefore, form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is also nothing but mind;
there is no separate, distinct emptiness. Even if there were a single dharma that transcended *nirvāṇa*, I would likewise [regard it as such].
It is said to be like an illusion and like a dream; therefore, emptiness is not different from form (*rūpa*). Since it is stated that they are not different, they are already mutually identical.
Yet, fearing that those whose minds are still bound by delusion might still interpret this as a mere matter of turning one's hand over or under, [the text] reiterates:
"Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. This means that whichever atom of form one picks up, its essence is immediately the horizontal pervasiveness of the *dharmadhātu*.
It is pervasive, vertical, and exhaustive; therefore, it is emptiness. This is what is meant by "the entirety of phenomena is identical to principle.

There is not the slightest bit of the nature of principle that does not reside within these phenomena. Thus, this very true emptiness contained within a single atom—the entirety of principle—immediately and completely possesses the entirety of the phenomena of the Dharma-realm;
therefore, it is form. As for the so-called "entirety of principle is identical to phenomena," there is not the slightest bit [of phenomenon] that is excluded.
Phenomenal characteristics do not exist within this principle; rather, it is the very substance itself that is free from dependence, such that no two things exist.

Once one has thoroughly realized this true mark (*dharmatā*) regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the same can be understood by analogy for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskāra, vijñāna*).

Furthermore, fearing that those who are deluded and attached might claim that this true mark of the five aggregates arises from the act of contemplative insight, he further provides this clarification.
It is said: These dharmas of the five aggregates are, in their very essence, the true mark of emptiness. They have been thus from the beginning;

it is not that the five aggregates cease because a mark of non-substantiality arises. Since the five aggregates are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, they are merely called "the mark of emptiness.
Furthermore, fearing that those who are deluded might think that although this mark of emptiness of the five aggregates is not subject to birth and extinction, it nonetheless...
Regarding defilement and purity: ordinary beings become defiled by following defiled conditions, while noble ones become pure by following pure conditions.

Therefore, it is further explained and shown: "The five aggregates of ordinary beings are themselves the mark of emptiness; the five aggregates of noble ones are themselves the mark of emptiness. What defilement or purity could there be?
Furthermore, fearing that those who are deluded might think this mark of emptiness of the five aggregates [is something other than the aggregates themselves], [it is said:]...

Although it is stainless and pure, there is increase and decrease. This means that because ordinary beings are deluded, birth and death are vast and expansive, which constitutes "increase," while their virtuous marks are obscured and concealed, which constitutes "decrease.
Because sages have awakened, their illuminating function is inexhaustible, which constitutes "increase," and their afflictions and karma have been extinguished, which constitutes "decrease.
Therefore, to further clarify this, it is said: "In the state of delusion, it is likewise only these dharmas in their aspect of emptiness; upon awakening..."
At that time, it is likewise only these dharmas with their mark of emptiness; what increase or decrease could there be?

Having already elucidated this wondrous truth regarding the five aggregates, he then extensively traverses all differentiated dharmic characteristics, dissolving and severing the emotional views of both the holy and the ordinary, stating:
"Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, and so on, up to no attainment. However, as for what is called...

From the formless realms down to the absence of even an "attainer," how could it be that these become non-existent only after being dissolved and severed? This is truly because there is fundamentally nothing to be attained.
That which is fundamentally unattainable is called the Truth (*satya*). To realize this state of non-attainment is called Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, none of these—be they the objects, the Truth, or the Contemplation—are ever separate from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the object of contemplation. Whether as the object, the Truth, or the Contemplation...
In total, these do not depart from the present moment of thought—the infinitesimal mind. This single mind fully possesses three meanings: "Truth" (di) is the true mark (*dharmatā*);

"Contemplation" (guan) is the illuminating observation; and "Object" (jing) is the written word. They are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither conjoined nor separate, and neither identical nor different.
Therefore, it is called the profound Prajñā.
Bodhisattvas, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have no hindrance in their minds. Because they have no hindrance, they are free from fear.
They are far removed from inverted thoughts and delusions, and they attain ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three periods of time rely on the [Prajñāpāramitā].
Because it is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Therefore, know that the perfection of wisdom is a great mantra of spiritual power, a great mantra of illumination, an unsurpassed mantra, and a mantra equal to the unequaled;
it is able to eliminate all suffering, being true and not false.
This universally cites all Bodhisattvas and Buddhas as witnesses to clarify that this profound Prajñā is truly able to deliver one from all suffering and distress.
That is to say: "The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate; the Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter its perfect clarity;
those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this Dharma. It is not merely a matter of contemplation.
This is Avalokiteśvara. When there is no obstruction, then karmic bonds are themselves liberation; this is the ultimate *upāya-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*.
When there is no fear, then the fruit of suffering is itself the *dharmakāya*; this is the ultimate *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*.

When one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, then afflictions are themselves wisdom-illumination; this is the ultimate *pariśuddha-nirvāṇa*. This is based upon the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
One attains the Bodhi of True Nature by relying on the *prajñā* of contemplative insight; one attains the Bodhi of Real Wisdom by relying on the *prajñā* of words and letters;
and one attains the Bodhi of Skillful Means [by relying on the *prajñā* of practice]. Bodhi is the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*);

wisdom must be in profound accord with principle. Nirvāṇa is the principle of suchness; principle must be in perfect harmony with wisdom. Therefore, they are described in relation to one another through mutual implication. This profound *prajñā* is...
It is a great divine mantra because it possesses wondrous efficacy; it is a great illuminating mantra because its wisdom manifests as light;
it is the unsurpassed mantra because it is the essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);

and it is the mantra equal to the unequaled because there is not a single dharma that can equal this mind, yet this mind can equal all dharmas by causing them to return together to the seal of the true mark. This heart-mantra is precisely...
This [mantra] is capable of eliminating the causes and effects of the various sufferings of both the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) types for oneself and others;
it is true and not false, and should be believed with earnest faith. Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-mantra is spoken. The mantra is as follows: *gate gate pāragate*.
*Tāttā*. *Pāra-saṃgatāttā*. *Bodhi svāhā*.
Since the preceding explicit teaching already indicates that Prajñāpāramitā is itself the mantra, one must understand that this esoteric teaching is that the mantra is itself Prajñāpāramitā.
However, the reason it is taught both explicitly and esoterically is that each—explicit and esoteric—possesses the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*. This is the correct [view].
It is best not to translate [the title]; it is inappropriate to engage in forced interpretation.
*The Essential Explanation of the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom* (End).
